sights.w: The most imposing survivor of Metz's medieval walls — a double gate and bridge over the Seille, its two 13th-century round towers joined to 15th-century gun bastions. Named for the Teutonic Knights who kept a hospital nearby; classified a historic monument, restored and reopened in 2014 with free access and exhibitions.

sights.address: 2 Rue du Haut Poirier, 57000 Metz, France
sights.w: Named for the vanished palace of the kings of Austrasia, this 6,000 m² museum walks 2,000 years of Metz history with free admission — one of France's great Gallo-Roman collections (thermal baths preserved in situ, the Merten column, a Mithra altar), Merovingian sculpture from Saint-Pierre-aux-Nonnains, and a fine-arts gallery.

sights.address: 1 Place du Général de Gaulle, 57000 Metz, France
sights.w: Repeatedly voted France's most beautiful railway station, this 1908 Rhenish-Romanesque colossus (350 m long, the longest in France) was built under Kaiser Wilhelm II to stamp a German imperial identity on annexed Metz. Cathedral-like stained glass, a high tower, and carved arabesques crown the heart of the Quartier Impérial; a historic monument since 1975.

Ricardo Bofill's 1989 concert hall, now Arsenal-Jean-Marie-Rausch, whose Grande Salle is prized for exceptional acoustics — Rostropovich called it 'fantastic' at the opening. The complex folds in exhibition galleries and two remarkable monuments: the 4th-century Saint-Pierre-aux-Nonnains and the 12th-century Templars' Chapel.

sights.address: 4-5 Place de la Comédie, 57000 Metz, France
sights.w: The oldest working opera house in France, inaugurated in 1752 on the elegant classical Place de la Comédie amid the water of the Moselle. Neo-classical and intimate, it is one of the last French houses to keep both a permanent choir and a ballet company.

A modest Outre-Seille church holding an outsized treasure: the last stained glass Jean Cocteau ever made, 24 windows across 14 bays created in 1961-63 — one of only three religious works of his life. Listed by Atlas Obscura among the places to see before you die.

sights.address: 1 Rue de la Citadelle, 57000 Metz, France
sights.w: Reputed the oldest church in France: a Gallo-Roman civil basilica of around 390 AD, turned into a church for a Benedictine convent in the 7th century — hence 'aux Nonnains'. Its white-limestone chancel is the most important preserved in France; today a monument and living cultural space beside the Arsenal.

Metz's most atmospheric old quarter, still medieval in feel below the towers of the Porte des Allemands — colombage houses, antiquarian and bookbinder shops, oriental grocers, and a young, bohemian crowd filling its bars, bistros and restaurants. The mid-September Foire à la Brocante is a local fixture.

The liveliest café square in the pedestrian heart of Metz, between Rue Fabert and Rue Ladoucette near the cathedral — terraces spilling out in the warm months, wooden chalets and mulled wine at Christmas.

sights.n: Plan d'Eau de Metz & Lac aux Cygnes
sights.w: A great artificial basin created in the 1970s where the Moselle splits the city — the Plan d'eau Saint-Symphorien on one bank, the Lac aux Cygnes park (a vestige of the old defensive moat) on the other. A favourite loop for walking, running and rowing, ringed by ramparts and the university's Île du Saulcy.

Four hectares of greenhouses, French parterres and romantic landscape founded in 1802 and moved here in 1865 around the 1719 Frescatelly summer pavilion — a century-old arboretum of ginkgos, sequoias and bald cypress, a rose garden and scent garden. Labelled 'Jardin remarquable' in 2025.

sights.address: Rue du Fort de Queuleu, 57070 Metz, France
sights.w: A fort built in 1868-70 to defend Metz that the Gestapo turned into an internment and transit camp in 1943-44, where 1,500-1,800 resisters and deportees were held before deportation. Now the regional memorial to resistance and deportation, with guided casemate visits and a wooded park open daily.

A former convent on the Sainte-Croix hill turned cult music venue — an intimate vaulted 'Caveau', a chapel and an open cloister that made Metz a French home of jazz in the 1970s-80s, hosting Sonny Rollins and Archie Shepp, and still programming jazz, rock and chanson today.

One of the most beautiful squares in the world and a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1983, built 1752-55 for Stanislas Leszczynski, deposed king of Poland turned Duke of Lorraine. Emmanuel Héré's harmonious ensemble is framed by Jean Lamour's gilded wrought-iron gates and Guibal's fountains.

Built 1901-02 by architect Henri Sauvage for cabinetmaker Louis Majorelle, one of the very few Art Nouveau houses still standing in France and a total work of the École de Nancy — staircase and stained glass by Jacques Gruber, ironwork, fireplaces and furniture in flowing plant motifs. Visited on reservation.

sights.address: 36-38 Rue du Sergent Blandan, 54000 Nancy, France
sights.w: The museum of the Art Nouveau movement founded in 1901 by Gallé, Prouvé, Majorelle and Daum — over 400 pieces of Gallé glass plus ceramics, furniture and the Daum manufacture's work, staged in period rooms (bedroom, dining room, office) to evoke the atmosphere of 1900.

On Place Stanislas in an 18th-century Héré pavilion, a rich gallery from Perugino and Caravaggio to Rubens and Delacroix — with an exceptional 20th-century holding, a Jean Prouvé room, and 300-odd Daum glass pieces shown around the Haussonville bastion in the basement.

The soaring neo-Gothic basilica of 1864-71 by Prosper Morey anchors Nancy's compact Ville Vieille — a medieval quarter of the Palais Ducal, Porte de la Craffe and cobbled lanes running between the old gate and the Arc Héré.
A 14th-century fortified gate closing the north end of the Ville Vieille, one of Nancy's oldest monuments and a vivid witness to the medieval city's military past.

sights.n: Palais des ducs de Lorraine – Musée Lorrain (Nancy)
sights.w: The ducal palace of Lorraine with its flamboyant portal and the Cordeliers church-convent, holding 155,000 works on the region's history from prehistory to today. A major renovation runs to 2027 (the Cordeliers church, with the dukes' tombs, stays open during works).

Twenty-one hectares of wooded promenade and a celebrated rose garden right beside Place Stanislas — a former royal nursery laid out by Stanislas on the old ducal gardens and opened to the public in 1835, now with an animal park, playgrounds and terraces.

Nancy's 18th-century cathedral, begun in 1703 under Duke Léopold and continued by Stanislas, notable for its grand Dupont organ transformed by Cavaillé-Coll into a symphonic instrument of four keyboards and 65 stops. Free daily visits.

The vast 1932 ossuary above the Verdun battlefield holds the remains of some 130,000 unidentified French and German soldiers, its national cemetery of 16,000 crosses stretching below. Where Mitterrand and Kohl clasped hands in 1984; part of the UNESCO WWI funerary and memorial sites since 2023, and the most visited monument in Lorraine.

sights.address: 1 Avenue du Corps Européen, 55100 Fleury-devant-Douaumont, France
sights.w: A modern museum on the site of the destroyed village of Fleury dedicated to the 1916 Battle of Verdun and its soldiers — immersive reconstructions of the battlefield, personal testimony, film and a deep collection of period objects, the essential place to understand the war of attrition that cost 700,000 casualties.

sights.address: Avenue du 5e Régiment d'Artillerie à Pied, 55100 Verdun, France
sights.w: Four kilometres of galleries dug beneath Verdun's citadel that became an underground city in 1916 — its ovens baking 28,000 rations a day and sheltering 2,000 men. Visited today in a self-guided car with augmented-reality glasses that reconstruct soldiers' daily life; here the Unknown Soldier was chosen in 1920.

sights.n: Musée de la Guerre de 1870 et de l'Annexion (Gravelotte)
sights.w: Europe's only museum wholly devoted to the Franco-Prussian War and the 1871-1918 annexation of Alsace-Moselle, opened in 2014 on the very ground of the August 1870 battles of Gravelotte and Saint-Privat. Some 6,000 objects — paintings, sculpture, press, testimony — across the memorial site facing the Halle du Souvenir.

An 11th-century fortress on a rocky spur above a Moselle bend at the three-borders point, one of the favourite residences of the Dukes of Lorraine and reputedly the only 11th-century castle with its walls, casemates and outer works still intact. Medieval re-enactments and craft workshops in season.

A quadrangular 15th-century fortress with powerful corner towers near the three-borders region, begun around 1419 by Arnold VI of Sierck and nicknamed for the Duke of Marlborough of the famous song. Classified in 1930, it stages large seasonal art and culture exhibitions along a six-century discovery trail.

A medieval bourg 6 km from Luxembourg, classed among the Plus Beaux Villages de France since 1987 and nicknamed 'the little Lorraine Carcassonne' — still ringed by 700 m of 15th-century ramparts up to 9 m high, with cobbled lanes, the 1560 Maison des Baillis and a hilltop citadel.

The story of 'white gold' in the Saulnois, where salty springs were worked on a near-industrial scale from the Iron Age — 20,000 tonnes a year. Housed in a Vauban fortified gate, the Porte de France, and renewed with 3D headsets, tablets and a virtual-reality reconstruction of the citadel.

sights.n: Musée départemental Georges de La Tour (Vic-sur-Seille)
sights.w: In the Saulnois birthplace of the great Baroque master of candlelight, a museum built around its prize — La Tour's 'Saint-Jean-Baptiste dans le désert' — with 960 m² of French painting from the 17th to early 20th century (Le Brun, Stella, Valenciennes, Corot).

The 12th-century keep of Thionville's feudal castle — its odd name a garbling of the Frankish for 'tower at the well' — now the municipal museum, telling the town's story from prehistory to the Renaissance across eight thematic rooms, near the market-square belfry and its two-tonne bell 'Grosse Suzanne'.

Between Metz and Thionville, one of France's densest leisure clusters set in forest — a European-scale zoo of nearly 2,000 animals across 18 hectares, France's only indoor ski slope, an aquarium, an Olympic ice rink and the Thermapolis thermal baths on iron-rich hot springs.

The largest Maginot Line artillery fortress, built 1929-35 — nineteen surface blocks linked by kilometres of underground galleries, ammunition stores, kitchens and a power plant, reached on an electric train inside the rock. Two-hour guided visits at a constant 12°C, culminating in the combat blocks and their turrets.

sights.n: Moulin de la Blies – Musée des Techniques Faïencières (Sarreguemines)
sights.address: 125 Avenue de la Blies, 57200 Sarreguemines, France
sights.w: Voted the French people's 9th favourite monument in 2015, the former paste-preparation mill of the great Sarreguemines pottery (1825-1969) now shows the machines and tools of faience-making, wrapped in the seven-part Jardin des Faïenciers laid out over the industrial ruins on the Blies riverbank.

sights.n: Musée des Émaux et Faïences de Longwy
sights.w: In Longwy-Haut, the city of the famous crackle-glaze enamels, a museum in a former military bakery tracing two crafts — faience made from 1798 and the celebrated cloisonné-style enamels from the 1870s — including the 200-piece Vernaujou-Brunet collection of Longwy enamels.
